title: Alain Badiou
keyWorks: Ethics: An Essay on the Understanding of Evil (1993)
summary: Alain Badiou is a French philosopher for whom the heart of life is the "event": an unexpected encounter, discovery or rupture after which the world can no longer stay the same. A person truly becomes a subject when they remain "faithful" to such an event and build their life out of it. Badiou identifies four domains in which truths are born: love, art, science and politics.
onEmotions: Badiou is not a psychologist and hardly writes about feelings as inner states. What interests him is what a person does when something happens to them that goes beyond the usual order of things. In his early Theory of the Subject, drawing on Lacan, he names four "affects" of the subject: anxiety, the superego, courage and justice. For Badiou, feelings are often signs that something new has broken into a life, or that a person is wavering between their habitual life and fidelity to this new thing. His view is supportive: even a difficult feeling can be a sign that you are living not only to survive, but for something greater.

anxiety.text: Badiou liked to repeat Lacan's line: anxiety is the one affect that does not deceive. If the unknown is making you queasy right now, that is hard, and there is nothing to be ashamed of. In Theory of the Subject he described anxiety as one of the four fundamental affects of the subject. Anxiety, for Badiou, arises when the usual order of things breaks down and something breaks into life that we don't yet have a name for. It is a sign of a collision with the new. But in the same book Badiou names another affect — courage: the ability to act without complete certainty. So your anxiety is not a verdict but a possible threshold. It tells you that something is changing. You don't need to get rid of it at once; alongside it you can find a little courage for one small step.
anxiety.practice: Stand up and take one step forward — literally, with your feet — saying to yourself: "I don't know what's there, and I'm going anyway." Badiou called this courage: movement without guarantees.

fear.text: Courage, Badiou wrote in Theory of the Subject, is not the absence of fear but the capacity to hold on to the new when your usual footing has vanished. You are afraid — and that is an honest response to the unknown. For Badiou, most of our life takes place within the order of the "situation" — the world of the familiar, where everything is known and assigned its place. An event disrupts this order, and fear is a natural response to such a disruption. Perhaps your fear indicates that you are facing something truly important. Courage, for Badiou, doesn't require you to stop being afraid. It only invites you not to let fear decide everything for you — and to take a step even if your knees are shaking.
fear.practice: Imagine one ordinary day in which your fear is present but doesn't decide for you. What would you do differently on that day? You don't have to do it — just take a look at such a day.

sadness.text: "Which life am I living right now — the life of the 'human animal' or the life of a subject?" Badiou would probably begin with that question, though he never wrote about sadness as such. Your sadness deserves to be listened to rather than hidden. He distinguished the life of the "human animal", concerned with survival and pleasures, from the life of a subject bound to something greater — love, creative work, a shared cause, the search for truth. Sadness often appears when we feel that life has been reduced to routine and that this something greater is missing. Such sadness is a longing for meaning. Badiou believed that every person has the capacity to become a subject of truth. Your sadness may be a reminder of this capacity — that you need not only comfort, but something genuine.
sadness.practice: Go through, in your mind, the four domains where, for Badiou, truths are born: love, art, science, a shared cause. For each, recall one moment from your own life. Which of the four are you missing most right now?

grief.text: "Fidelity to the event" is what Badiou called the capacity to go on living out of what once changed your life, even when the event itself lies in the past. The grief you carry deserves time and respect. If you have lost a person, or something that was an event for you — a love, a friendship, a shared cause — the loss does not cancel what happened. The event took place, and it goes on acting through you: through the way you see the world, what you value, how you live. Grief is the price of that bond, and paying it hurts. Fidelity to what was lost doesn't have to mean freezing in pain; it can mean carrying forward what you were given — at your own pace.
grief.practice: Today, do one small thing the way the one you lost would have done it: brew their kind of tea, walk their route, use their favourite word. Badiou would call this fidelity: the event goes on through you.

loneliness.text: Badiou called love a "scene of the Two" and spent his life thinking about how the Two is born out of the One. Loneliness hurts precisely because the need for such a scene is alive in you. In In Praise of Love he describes love as a "scene of the Two": an experience in which the world begins to be seen not from one point of view but from two. But Badiou stresses something else too: the truths born in love, art, science and politics are universal — they are addressed to everyone. So even in loneliness you are not cut off from what is shared. When you read a book, listen to music or think through a real question, you take part in something that connects people. And loneliness can become a waiting for an encounter — an openness to an event.
loneliness.practice: Open a book or a poem you love and read one line aloud — slowly, as if to someone in the room. Badiou held that the truth of art is addressed to "anyone at all": for this minute there are already two of you — you and the one who wrote it.

anger.text: Badiou counted justice among the four affects of the subject — alongside anxiety, the superego and courage. Your anger most likely tells you that something just has been violated, and it is worth listening to. But in Ethics he also warns about forms of evil that arise when fidelity to something great turns into destruction: when, for the sake of their truth, a person is ready to destroy others. He calls this the "terror" and "disaster" of truth. As a signal of injustice it is valuable, but its force calls for clarity. Badiou would help you tell apart anger that strives for justice for everyone from anger that only wants to win or take revenge. The first can become a source of faithful action; the second tends to wear out both you and others.
anger.practice: Say one sentence aloud to someone you trust: "It makes me angry that…, because it is unjust towards…". Badiou distinguished anger that wants to win from anger that wants justice for everyone — spoken aloud, the difference is easier to hear.

shame.text: In Ethics, Badiou argues against the habit of seeing a person above all as a victim — a weak creature to be protected and assessed. Shame is agonizing, and you deserve gentleness towards yourself within it. For Badiou, every person has a capacity for something more: to become a subject bound to a truth — in love, in creative work, in thought, in a shared cause. Shame often reduces us to one mistake or one trait, as if our whole essence lay in it. Badiou invites you to see a person differently: as someone capable of fidelity, of a new beginning. Your mistake doesn't define your whole life — you are more than what you are ashamed of.
shame.practice: Imagine looking at your mistake through the eyes of someone who believes in you — a friend, a teacher, a grandparent. What would they see in you besides it? Stay with that answer for at least a minute.

guilt.text: "Keep going!" — that is Badiou's entire ethical maxim for someone who has once lost their way. The guilt you feel shows that you care. In Ethics, Badiou calls one form of evil "betrayal" — giving up fidelity to an event that once changed your life: a love, a cause, a discovery. But in his view fidelity is not a flawless past; it is something that can be renewed. A subject is not created once and for all, but with each new decision to keep going. If you feel guilty for stepping back from something important, it doesn't mean all is lost. The guilt itself shows that the bond with that important thing is still alive. You can turn it not into self-punishment but into a return — the next step of fidelity.
guilt.practice: Today, take one tiny step back towards what you stepped away from: one message, one page, five minutes. Badiou would call this renewing fidelity — it demands no atonement, only the next step.

envy.text: "The service of goods" is what Badiou, following Lacan, called a life built around acquiring, owning and comparing. If envy is stinging you right now, it is honest to admit it — it is a very human feeling. In that world there will always be someone who has more. But the truths Badiou writes about work differently: they belong to no one and don't diminish when they are shared. Someone else's love doesn't take away your ability to love; someone else's discovery doesn't close off yours. Envy torments us as long as we live by the logic of goods. But it can point to what really matters to you — and then the question is no longer "why do they have it and I don't" but "what do I want to be faithful to?".
envy.practice: In your mind, sort what you envy into two piles: what here is a "good" that can be owned, and what is a cause one can devote oneself to? The second pile is your clue.

emptiness.text: "There are only bodies and languages" — this is how Badiou, in Logics of Worlds, sums up the core conviction of our time, adding: "except that there are truths." The emptiness you feel is heavy, and it deserves attention rather than reproach. Badiou might explain it like this: a life without an event is a life reduced to keeping oneself going — to work, rest and consumption. Your emptiness is not an emptiness of you yourself, but a sense that nothing truly new has happened in your life for a long time. Badiou doesn't suggest manufacturing events artificially — they arrive unexpectedly. But you can stay open to them: to an encounter, an idea, a cause that might suddenly take hold of you.
emptiness.practice: Go out for five minutes without your phone and look for just one thing on the way: something you have never noticed here before. Badiou believed the new arrives unexpectedly — train your eye for it.

confusion.text: An event, Badiou says, is "undecidable": at the moment it happens, it cannot be proven that it truly matters. That is why confusion is its frequent companion, and there is nothing shameful in it. A first meeting, an unexpected thought, a sharp turn — all of these at first bring disarray, even to the most decisive people. There are no rules to tell you what to do, and no guarantee that the choice will prove right. The subject, for Badiou, is born out of a decision, a kind of wager — a choice made without full certainty. Your confusion is not an absence of bearings but a sign that you are facing something new. Clarity will come not before the decision, but through it.
confusion.practice: If you are facing a small choice, toss a coin — not so that it decides, but to notice which side you were secretly hoping for while it was in the air. Badiou said the subject is born of a wager: this is your first piece of knowledge about yourself.

fatigue.text: Fidelity to an event, for Badiou, is not a heroic impulse but long, everyday work — persistence over time. Your tiredness is real, and it doesn't diminish what you are doing. Such fidelity is naturally tiring. But it is worth distinguishing two kinds of tiredness: tiredness from the "service of goods" — from the endless race for possessions and status — and tiredness from fidelity to what truly matters to you. The first exhausts you because it has no end, while the second, for all its heaviness, is full of meaning. Badiou doesn't demand superhuman strength from you. Fidelity includes pauses and rest too — you can only keep going by taking care of yourself.
fatigue.practice: Lie or sit down for three minutes, doing nothing, and in your mind let go of every "I must" except one that is truly yours. Fidelity, for Badiou, includes the pause: rest is part of carrying on too.

boredom.text: The "state of the situation" is Badiou's name for the familiar order in which everything has already been counted and assigned its place, and each day is like the one before. Boredom in such a world is hard to bear, and there is nothing shameful in it. Here nothing really happens: there is only a recount of what already exists. Boredom is the sense that life consists of repetition while you are waiting for something more. And that waiting isn't empty, even if right now it drags on painfully. Badiou believed that events arrive unexpectedly, from points the order doesn't notice. Your boredom may be a form of openness — a waiting, not in vain, for something that will one day break the monotony and call you to follow it.
boredom.practice: Break one habitual route today: take a different street, sit in a different chair, drink your tea from a different cup. Badiou said an event comes from a point the order doesn't notice — give such a point a chance.

joy.text: Satisfaction and happiness are not the same thing, Badiou insists in Metaphysics of Real Happiness. The joy you have right now needs no justification. Satisfaction is when our needs and comforts are met, when everything goes as it should. Happiness, for Badiou, is tied to an event: it arises when we take part in something new — in love, a discovery, creative work, a shared cause — and find in ourselves abilities we never suspected. It may be a sign that you have touched something genuine. It is worth noticing it and asking yourself where it came from. Perhaps it is not just a pleasant moment but the beginning of something you can be faithful to.
joy.practice: Tell someone about your joy — not for praise, but to name aloud where it came from. Badiou held that happiness, unlike satisfaction, is bound up with what can be shared.

love.text: Badiou saw "I love you" not as mere words but as a declaration: the moment a chance encounter starts turning into fidelity. He would take your tenderness seriously — he devoted a whole book to it, In Praise of Love. For him, love begins with an encounter — an event that cannot be predicted and that breaks through ordinary life. But the main thing is not the encounter but what follows it: the long, shared work of building a world "from the point of view of the Two". Badiou criticizes today's attempts to make love safe, free of risk, choosing a partner like a product. Love, in his view, is an adventure that demands tenacity. Your tenderness is not just a pleasant feeling but the beginning or continuation of a truth that is created by two people. It is worth cherishing as an event that changed how you see the world.
love.practice: Look at one thing together with someone you love — out of the window, at the street, at an old photo — and ask what they see. Badiou called this the "scene of the Two": the world seen from two points at once.

quote.author: Arthur Rimbaud
quote.source: A Season in Hell (Badiou quotes these words in In Praise of Love)

gratitude.text: Badiou, a convinced atheist, borrowed the word "grace" from the apostle Paul, freeing it from its religious sense, to name what is given without being deserved. The gratitude you feel answers precisely to such gifts. An event, for Badiou, cannot be produced, earned or planned: it happens, it arrives on its own. Meeting someone you love, an unexpected idea, a book that changed your life — all of these are gifts that might never have come. Gratitude in this sense is the recognition that the best things in our lives came not only from our own efforts. This view lightens the load: you don't have to earn all the good that has happened to you. You can simply accept it — and give thanks.
gratitude.practice: Say "thank you" to one person for something they may not even have noticed: a meeting, a sentence, simply being there. For Badiou the best things arrive as grace — naming it aloud is how you recognize it.

hope.text: Badiou disliked passively waiting for everything to sort itself out somehow — and yet it is hard to find a more hopeful philosopher. It's good that you have hope: he would show you what it can rest on. His thought affirms that the new is possible, that events happen even where nobody expects them, and that every person is capable of taking part in something greater. In Ethics he formulates a simple maxim for anyone who has once touched something important: "Keep going!" This is not about straining yourself but about calm persistence. Your hope, then, is not a dream of a future someone else will bring, but fidelity to what has already been promised to you by an encounter, a cause, a love. To hope is to keep going, even in small steps.
hope.practice: Say one word aloud to yourself — "Keep going!" — and at once make a small move towards what you hope for: open the file, dial the number, step over the threshold. Badiou considered this word the whole of ethics.

quote.text: Do all that you can to persevere in that which exceeds your perseverance.
quote.author: Alain Badiou
quote.source: Ethics: An Essay on the Understanding of Evil

nostalgia.text: Badiou would suggest telling nostalgia and fidelity apart: one looks back, the other forward. There is no need to stifle this warm, aching longing for the past. Nostalgia faces backwards: it longs for what was and wants to bring the past back. Fidelity to an event, for Badiou, faces forwards: it takes what once happened and keeps unfolding its consequences in the present and the future. Your nostalgia may hold the memory of an event — a love, a friendship, a time when you felt truly alive. That is a precious memory. And you can turn it from longing into a question: how can what mattered then continue in my life now?
nostalgia.practice: Put on a song from the time you miss and listen to it to the end, doing nothing else. When it finishes, ask: what from that time can I carry on today?

craving.text: Logics of Worlds has Badiou's notion of a "point": the moment when the whole world seems to shrink to a simple "yes" or "no". An acute craving feels exactly like that, and the fact that it's hard for you says nothing bad about you. Badiou distinguishes the "human animal", which lives by its interests, habits and needs, from the "subject" — the same person at a moment when they hold on to something greater than the immediate. This is no reproach to the animal in us: everyone has it. But Badiou stresses that a subject is made not of one heroic gesture but of many small decisions. One wave is not the whole world, and it passes.
craving.practice: When the wave comes, say aloud or to yourself: "This is a point, not the whole world." Then do one small thing — a sip of water, a few steps — and notice how the wave changes.

addiction.text: "Democratic materialism" was Badiou's name for the climate of an age in which life is reduced to "bodies and languages", to consumption and the satisfaction of needs. Seen this way, addiction is not a moral failure, not a life sentence and not only a personal fault, but a circuit that is genuinely hard to get out of. It can be seen as a world that has narrowed and arranged itself around a single centre. Badiou believes that in any situation, even the most closed, something new is possible, and that truths are not built alone: for Badiou, a subject can also be collective. The way out of the circuit is not a single burst of willpower but a slow fidelity to what makes life wider again, together with other people.
addiction.practice: Tell one person — a friend, or someone in a mutual-help group — about something that once truly captivated you, other than what your life is built around now. Badiou held that a subject can be collective: the way out of the circuit is easier to build together.

hangover.text: Badiou refused to see a person through their worst moment — he looked at what a person is capable of next. The morning after can be doubly hard: your body feels bad, and inside you feel anxious and ashamed — but none of this makes you a worse person. In Ethics, Badiou says that fidelity is not flawlessness but the capacity to keep going. His ethical maxim is simple: keep going, hold on to what matters to you, even if you've lost your way. Last night doesn't define who you are. Memory gaps and awkwardness can be frightening, but today is not a continuation of yesterday's failure; it is a new chance to choose what you stay faithful to.
hangover.practice: Drink a glass of water slowly, in small sips, and with each sip name to yourself one thing you are holding on to today. Fidelity, for Badiou, is not flawlessness but carrying on.

euphoria.text: The world suddenly seems open, anything is possible — Badiou wrote like no one else about such moments, when something new breaks into life. There's no need to spoil this high with suspicion. But he offers one distinction: an event is recognized not by the strength of its first impression, but by what is later built from it. An intense feeling may be the sign of a genuine encounter, idea or love — or it may simply be a bright moment, and there's nothing wrong with that either. You can calmly enjoy the high and at the same time look with curiosity: what in it is truly yours, and what will you want to carry on once the wave settles?
euphoria.practice: While the high lasts, write down one thought or image that seems important, and date it. Reread it in a couple of days: Badiou would say an event is tested by what carries on from it.

crash.text: After May 1968, Badiou wrote, came a "Restoration": the familiar order returned, and it seemed as if nothing had ever happened. A comedown after a high is like that on a small scale: a moment ago everything was bright, and now it is grey and heavy, and it hurts. Badiou saw this rhythm throughout history: flashes of the new are followed by periods of return. But for Badiou this does not cancel the event: it took place, and its consequences keep acting. The comedown is not proof that the high was a deception. It is a time when the flash has ended and the slow work has not yet begun. You can let this time be, without demanding of yourself that you bring back the earlier brightness right away.
crash.practice: Give yourself ten minutes of quiet "restoration" with no demands: tea, a blanket, a window. Before you get up, name one thing from the recent high that was real and stays with you.

panic.text: Badiou, following Lacan, described anxiety as an encounter with something "excessive" — something that doesn't fit into the familiar order. Right now your heart is pounding and your breathing falters, and it is very frightening. You are not alone with this: a wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes, even if that is hard to believe right now. Beside anxiety Badiou places courage — not the absence of fear, but the capacity to stay put while something incomprehensible is happening. In a moment of panic you don't need to decide or understand anything. Courage here is very simple and bodily — waiting out the wave, feeling the ground under your feet and breathing, knowing that it passes.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor, as if taking your place, and take a few breaths with the out-breath longer than the in-breath. On each out-breath say to yourself: "I'm staying," until the wave begins to ebb.

dread.text: Badiou argued with Heidegger and with every philosophy that puts "being-towards-death" at the centre. The question "what is it all for, if everything ends?" is heavy, and there is a lot of honesty in it. He holds that a human being is defined not by being mortal, but by being able to take part in truths — in love, creative work, knowledge, a shared cause. In Ethics he even says that a human being can be "immortal": not because they won't die, but because in moments of fidelity to a truth they partake in something that goes beyond their individual life. The answer to "what for?", then, is not a formula but what you already love, understand and do together with others.
dread.practice: Close your eyes and spend a minute inside the memory of a moment when you were wholly absorbed in something — a conversation, music, a task. In it, Badiou would say, you were a little "immortal": the question "what for?" simply didn't arise.

fomo.text: "The true life is absent" — Badiou loved to quote this line by Rimbaud and named a book after it, The True Life. The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are not where you should be is very common, and it can spoil even a good evening. But for Badiou the true life is not "somewhere out there", in other people's bright events and photos. A real event, in his view, cannot be planned, bought or caught by scrolling a feed: it happens within your own situation, often where nobody is looking. The fear of missing out pushes you to chase other people's lives, while an event comes to the one who is open to what is happening right beside them.
fomo.practice: Put your phone down and spend five minutes simply looking around — out of the window, at the street, around the room. Find one thing that is happening right here and appears in no feed.

quote.text: True life is absent. We are not in the world.
quote.author: Arthur Rimbaud

sleepless.text: Badiou distinguished the "state of the situation" — the habitual order that counts everything, sorts it into boxes and evaluates it — from what does not fit into this order. In the small hours this recount is especially loud, and it is no wonder that you are struggling. At night everything seems bigger and more hopeless. Badiou would probably note that night thoughts resemble an endless recount: what hasn't been done, what went wrong. But this recount is not the truth about you. Badiou insists that the most important things in life can't be derived from calculations. At night you can allow yourself not to solve anything, and simply put off the counting until morning.
sleepless.practice: Put a hand on your chest and say to yourself: "The count is closed until morning." Then count not tasks but out-breaths — ten slow ones; if you lose track, simply start again.

betrayal.text: "Nothing really happened" — that, for Badiou, is what the betrayer tells themselves: in Ethics, betrayal is the renunciation of fidelity to what once changed a life. If you have been betrayed, what collapses is not only trust in a person but what you believed in together — and this pain is legitimate. But one thing matters: if someone betrayed you, it doesn't cancel what was genuine on your side. Your fidelity, your love or friendship were real. Badiou shows that betrayal is the other's renunciation, not proof that you were naive. You don't have to renounce what you saw back then and what you invested in.
betrayal.practice: Say aloud to yourself, calmly and all the way through: "What was real on my side was real." Badiou would call this fidelity to the event — another's renunciation cannot cancel it.

jealousy.text: The One against the Two — this is how Badiou describes the central tension of love. Jealousy is agonizing, and there is often more fear of loss in it than anger. In In Praise of Love, Badiou describes love as a "scene of the Two": two people don't merge into one, but begin to look at the world together from the point of view of difference. Jealousy is a moment when love pulls back towards "the One": towards the wish to possess, to control, to reduce the other to yourself. This doesn't make you a bad person: it is what fear sounds like. But for Badiou love is not possession but a shared construction that rests on trust and on risk. You can acknowledge jealousy without letting it decide for you: it speaks of fear, not necessarily of the truth.
jealousy.practice: If the moment is right, say to the person you love not "where were you?" but "I'm scared of losing you." Badiou held that love rests on trust and risk — this is a small risk of trust.

resentment.text: "The future cannot be derived from the past" — Badiou returned to this thought in book after book. An old grievance is heavy: you carry it for years, and you really were hurt. Badiou doesn't write directly about grievances, but in Ethics he criticizes a view in which a person is defined first and foremost as a victim — as someone to whom something was done. He doesn't deny real harm, but he holds that a person is more than their wounds: they are capable of something new. A grievance keeps you tied to one old situation, as if time had stopped. Badiou doesn't demand that you forgive or forget. He only reminds you that you have a right to a life defined not only by what was done to you.
resentment.practice: Give five minutes to something that has nothing to do with this grievance: a plant, a song, a short walk. For Badiou, this is a small way out of repetition.

heartbreak.text: Love, for Badiou, is one of the four domains in which truth is born, on a par with science, art and politics. So he would take your pain with complete seriousness: a broken heart hurts almost physically. In In Praise of Love he writes that love begins with an encounter — an event — and then becomes the long construction of a world seen through the eyes of two. A breakup interrupts this construction but does not cancel the fact that it existed. You saw the world from the point of view of the Two, and that vision has already changed you. Badiou considers love a risk you can't insure against — and that is exactly why it is precious. Your pain is the price of having taken that risk.
heartbreak.practice: Go for a short walk and notice on the way one thing you learned to see thanks to this relationship. That way of seeing, Badiou would say, stays yours.

impostor.text: "Anyone at all" — that, for Badiou, is who truths are addressed to: to take part in them you need no special status. The fear of being found out any minute is known even to those you admire — you are not alone in it. For him, a subject is not someone who possesses the right qualifications in advance, but someone who holds to fidelity to something new. The subject itself emerges in the process; it doesn't exist before it. The feeling of being "not the real thing" often means you are engaged in something bigger than your former role. Nobody is ever "ready" in advance. You become who you become by doing it.
impostor.practice: Read aloud the lines by Beckett, whom Badiou loved: "Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better." Nobody is ready in advance — the subject emerges in the process.

self_hatred.text: The superego, as Badiou describes it after Lacan, is the voice of a law that demands more and more, punishes, and is never satisfied. If such a voice is judging you mercilessly right now, remember: it sounds convincing, but it doesn't tell the whole truth about you. In Theory of the Subject it is one of the four affects of the subject. Alongside it Badiou places courage and justice — entirely different ways of relating to yourself and the world. The inner critic is not your conscience but a harsh mechanism that confuses high standards with cruelty. Its verdict is not final, however loudly it rings. Justice, for Badiou, concerns everyone — including you.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence of the inner critic, and next to it what a fair person who could see the whole picture would say. Justice, for Badiou, concerns everyone — including you.

helplessness.text: "We have been naught, we shall be all" — Badiou loved this line from the "Internationale". Feeling unable to change anything is hard, and it is often down to real circumstances rather than any weakness of yours. In Logics of Worlds, Badiou introduces the concept of "the inexistent": in every world there is something that is barely visible in it, that exists only minimally. An event, for Badiou, can raise this inexistent to full existence. What seems impossible now is not necessarily impossible forever. Badiou says that the new is often born precisely where the order declares "that can't happen". You don't have to change everything at once; sometimes it is enough to stay open.
helplessness.practice: Do one tiny thing that is definitely within your power: water a plant, answer one message, open a window. Badiou would call this a point where "the inexistent" begins to exist.

procrastination.text: Badiou described fidelity to an event as everyday work — not a heroic leap but carrying on, step by step. If you can't get started, it isn't laziness or a vice: often there is fear, tiredness or a sense that the task is too big. His maxim in Ethics sounds almost homely: keep going. Starting doesn't mean doing everything right straight away. Badiou stresses that the subject acts without guarantees: nobody knows in advance whether something will work out. Courage, in his view, is not confidence in success but a readiness to take a step when there is no certainty. Sometimes that step is very small — and that is exactly where everything begins.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for two minutes and do only the smallest part of the task — without guarantees, as Badiou would say. When the timer rings, decide whether to go on.

uprooted.text: "There is only one world" — Badiou's political thesis grew out of his work with migrant workers in France. A move, emigration, the loss of familiar ground — this is a real loss, and the pain of it is real. For Badiou, truths don't belong to one nation or culture — they are universal and open to everyone. Losing your ground does not take away your place in the world: there are no "natives" and "strangers" in it, only people who live here. You can carry with you what was an event for you — a love, a thought, a cause — and it remains yours in any language. The new place, too, can become a place of encounters — in time, without hurry.
uprooted.practice: Sing or murmur a line of a song, a poem or a saying in the language of the place you come from. For Badiou there is one world, and what was an event for you remains yours in any language.

overload.text: The feed is the perfect machine for what Badiou called the "state of the situation": an order that counts, names and sorts everything into opinions. The overload it causes is exhausting, and it is not your fault: that's how the environment is built. Every event there instantly turns into one more opinion, leaving almost no room for anything genuinely new. Badiou holds that behind the stream of "bodies and languages" it is easy to miss a truth — something genuinely new that can't be reduced to yet another opinion. Truth, in his view, is rare and requires concentration, not an endless stream. You can allow yourself to step out of the stream in order to notice the few things that really matter to you.
overload.practice: Close the feed and sit for three minutes in silence, filling it with nothing. Then ask: which one thought right now is truly mine, not something I've just heard? Badiou considered truth rare — it needs silence.

unreality.text: In Logics of Worlds, Badiou separates being from appearing: what is can appear in a particular world with different "intensity". The sense that everything somehow isn't real is strange and sometimes frightening, and it deserves gentle treatment. Existence in a world, for Badiou, is a matter of degree. The feeling of unreality resembles a moment when you, or the world around you, appear with very low intensity — muffled, as if from far away. But that doesn't mean you aren't there: you are here, the light is just dimmed for now. Badiou stresses that the degree of appearing can change. Often it is brought back by simple, concrete things: a touch, a voice, a familiar task.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a distinct texture — fabric, wood, cold water — and name the sensation in three words. This, in Badiou's terms, is how the world gradually regains its intensity.

awe.text: Infinity, for Badiou, is not God's privilege or an unreachable distance but an ordinary property of being — this is how he read Cantor's set theory. The awe you have felt is worth simply living through. For Cantor, as for Badiou, there is not even one infinity but infinitely many different ones. Awe is the moment when you suddenly notice this infinity right beside you — in the starry sky, in music, in another person's face. Badiou also considers art one of the four domains in which truth is born — and music or a painting can open onto the infinite as well as mathematics can. Your awe is not just an emotion but a sign of meeting something greater than the usual order.
awe.practice: Return your gaze to whatever filled you with awe — or go out and look at the sky — and do nothing for a minute. Just try to feel it: this is greater than any count.

relief.text: Badiou tied anxiety to the moment when the usual order cracks — which makes the moment when the tension finally lets go all the more precious. This quiet feeling can be allowed to be there fully. While anxiety held you, your whole body was braced for a blow; now you can unclench your fists. Fidelity, for Badiou, is long, everyday persistence, not a life of constant anxiety; there is room in it for a breather too. Relief shows how much strength was going into holding on. You can enjoy it without rushing to find the next task or a new reason to worry. A breather doesn't cancel what matters to you — it gives you the strength to keep going tomorrow.
relief.practice: Drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw and let out a slow breath, noticing where in your body things have eased. Tell yourself: "A breather is part of fidelity too."

calm.text: Badiou usually writes about stormy moments — events, decisions, ruptures. But what you feel right now, quiet and needing no earning, has its place in his thought too. Fidelity to an event, for Badiou, is not a series of flashes but a long, everyday continuation: quiet work, calm reliability, the day-to-day "holding on". Love for him is not only an encounter but also duration, a life shared over time. Calm can be exactly that kind of time: not emptiness, but the quiet steadiness of what you are faithful to — people, tasks, familiar joys. You can simply stay in it, adding nothing and not asking yourself whether you've done enough.
calm.practice: Sit still for a minute and name to yourself what in your life is steady and reliable right now. For Badiou, this is the quiet side of fidelity.

inspiration.text: "A throw of the dice will never abolish chance" — Badiou returned to this Mallarmé poem all his life. Your inspiration is like such a throw: something new has become possible. Badiou names art as one of the four domains in which truths are born, alongside love, science and politics. For him, inspiration can be understood as an encounter with an event: something unforeseen opens a new way of seeing or doing. But Badiou also stresses the second part: an event lives only through fidelity to it, through the work that follows the flash. Inspiration is not only a gift but also an invitation. You can enjoy it now and also take a first step so that it doesn't stay a mere moment. And it's all right if the flash fades later: for Badiou, fidelity rests not on the strength of a feeling but on carrying on.
inspiration.practice: Take the idea's first tiny step right now: a sketch, one call, one line. Badiou held that an event lives only through what follows it.

schadenfreude.text: The "human animal" cares about survival, advantage and its place among others — Badiou never shamed it, but he never took it for the whole person either. Schadenfreude is one of those feelings that are awkward to admit even to yourself, and yet it visits almost everyone. If we continue Badiou's thought, schadenfreude is the voice of precisely this animal: in a world where everything is compared, someone else's fall seems for a moment to lift us higher. There is nothing monstrous in this — only the logic of competition we are all built into. But Badiou reminds us that truths work differently: they don't divide people into winners and losers, and another's failure adds nothing to your life. Having noticed schadenfreude, you can ask: what race am I running right now — and do I need it?
schadenfreude.practice: Imagine the race is gone: no ranking, no comparison. What would happen to your schadenfreude in that moment — and what do you yourself actually want?

contempt.text: Saint Paul: The Foundation of Universalism is an unexpected book for an atheist, but Badiou saw in Paul a thinker for whom there is "neither Jew nor Greek". Contempt can be cold and convenient: it puts us above others and protects us from what hurt us. Badiou stresses that truth is addressed to all without exception, and in Ethics he affirms that any person is capable of becoming a subject, that is, of going beyond their habitual, "animal" life. Contempt passes a final verdict on what can be seen in a person so far, and forgets what they are capable of. At the same time, contempt often guards something precious in you — for example, your fidelity to honesty or to a cause. It helps to make out that value: then you can hold on to it without turning the other person into a nobody.
contempt.practice: Write: "What I despise in this person is…", and below it: "So what matters to me is…". The second line will tell you more about yourself than the first.

disgust.text: "The inexistent" is Badiou's name, in Logics of Worlds, for what is present in a world yet barely admitted into visibility, as if it weren't there. Disgust is a strong bodily reaction: you want to pull away, not see, not touch, and it isn't chosen. Badiou didn't write about disgust, but he would probably say that it pushes something into the zone of the inexistent: this must not appear. When disgust is turned on a part of yourself, it's as if you deny that part the right to exist. But for Badiou it is precisely the inexistent that may turn out to be the place where something new begins. Perhaps what makes you feel disgust with yourself deserves not banishment but an attentive, calm look.
disgust.practice: Notice where in your body the disgust lives — in your throat, your stomach, your shoulders — and breathe slowly out into that place. Then ask: what am I trying to push away from myself with this disgust?

revenge.text: Justice, for Badiou, is not returning the blow but creating something new in which the old injustice is no longer possible. The wish for revenge is usually born of real pain: you were treated unjustly, and something inside demands balance. In Theory of the Subject he names justice as one of the four affects of the subject. Revenge, by contrast, is built as repetition: it mirrors the wound and ties you to the one who inflicted it. Badiou is always interested in breaking with repetition. Acknowledging the wish for revenge is honest; listening to what it protects is useful. Usually beneath it lies the need to be recognized — for your pain to matter. That need can be respected without causing anyone harm.
revenge.practice: Imagine that justice has already been restored, and the one who hurt you has nothing to do with it: what would have changed in your life? Name the single most important word — that is what you truly need.

anger_at_loved.text: Love, Badiou says, is neither a merger nor an idyll, but a long construction in which the difference between two people never disappears. Anger at those close to us can be especially sharp, and shame often follows: how could I snap at someone I love? In In Praise of Love, Badiou describes love as a "scene of the Two": an experience in which the world is seen not from one point of view but from two different ones. Badiou was writing about couples, but if we continue his thought, it holds for any closeness: anger is a sign that there are two of you and that your views have collided. It doesn't refute love. Fidelity, for Badiou, is not the absence of conflicts but the return to the shared construction after them. Anger gives no right to wound, but it doesn't make you a bad person.
anger_at_loved.practice: Once things are calmer, start a conversation with the words: "At that moment I wanted you to see…". For Badiou, this is exactly the return to the shared construction.

ambivalence.text: The subject, for Badiou, is always split and never entirely whole — an idea he took from Lacan. So when you love someone and at the same time can't stand them, neither feeling has to be the "false" one. And love, for him, is a "scene of the Two" in which the difference between two people doesn't dissolve but keeps working. Mixed feelings are not a breakdown of love but a trace of that very difference: the other person never fully coincides with your expectations. Fidelity, for Badiou, doesn't require a single, pure feeling — it rests on the decision to keep going, not on the absence of doubts. You can let both feelings be and not hurry to choose between them.
ambivalence.practice: Take two slow breaths: on the first, silently name what you love in this person; on the second, what you can't stand. Decide nothing: for Badiou, fidelity rests not on the purity of a feeling but on the decision to keep going.

guilty_relief.text: Badiou refused to measure the worth of a life by how much a person has endured: in Ethics he argues against the cult of suffering and sacrifice. Relief after a breakup, a departure or even the death of a seriously ill loved one often comes with shame — and yet it is compatible with love. Badiou also has the notion of the "human animal" — the part of us that simply wants to survive, to rest, to stop being under strain. Relief is its legitimate voice. Relief and love live on different levels and don't cancel each other out. Your fidelity to what was real in that relationship continues regardless of what your body is breathing out right now.
guilty_relief.practice: Allow yourself one long out-breath — the one your body has been waiting for — and right after it, recall one thing that was real between you. Relief doesn't erase it.

indifference.text: Compassion on schedule was, for Badiou in Ethics, a mark of ready-made "consensus" morality, which prescribes in advance what to feel and when. Sometimes something "should" move you, yet inside all is quiet, and that feels awkward. For him, truth begins not with an obligatory emotion but with an event: an unexpected encounter that really takes hold of you. Events are rare; most of the time we live in the ordinary order of things, which Badiou calls the "state of the situation". Indifference is not a moral flaw but honest testimony: right now this hasn't taken hold of you. Faking a feeling is worse than admitting its absence. Sometimes indifference is tiredness, sometimes protection; either way it doesn't define who you are.
indifference.practice: Look out of the window for a couple of minutes, or step outside, and notice whatever touches you even slightly: a sound, a colour, someone's face. There's no need to fake a feeling — an event, for Badiou, takes hold of you by itself.

escape.text: Badiou distinguished a simple change of scenery from a real break — an event after which a new possibility appears. If you feel like dropping your job, your city, your usual role, it usually means your old life has become too tight, and that is an important signal. He called the habitual order of things the "state of the situation": everything in it is counted and put in its place, and sometimes there's no air to breathe. The dream of running away is a longing for an event, for something that will finally lead beyond what has been counted. Badiou gives no recipe for "leave or stay". But he offers a question: what do I want to be faithful to? The answer may turn out to matter more than an address — and hint at what change you really need.
escape.practice: Walk for ten minutes along an unfamiliar street near home, as if you were already in another city. What in this feeling do you actually need — a new address, or a new cause to be faithful to?

forbidden_attraction.text: Everything begins with an encounter, Badiou writes in In Praise of Love — with a chance that can't be planned or forbidden in advance. That is why being drawn to someone unavailable or "not the right one" is so unsettling: as if you aren't in charge of your own feelings — and in part, that's true. He distinguishes the event of the encounter itself from what comes after: a decision, a declaration, a long construction for which a person is responsible. Attraction in itself is neither an act nor a verdict, but a sign that something in you has responded. Badiou also distinguishes desire, which is directed at an image, from love, which is directed at the whole person. There's no need to rush to conclusions: you can simply explore what exactly in this encounter has touched you so much.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Imagine that this attraction is a letter addressed not to that person but to you. What life, what qualities is it telling you about?

social_anxiety.text: Every situation, for Badiou, has its "state" — a system of accounting that counts everyone and places them in the right box. Under other people's gaze this feels almost physical: it seems as if someone is weighing your every step, and that is exhausting. But for Badiou a subject can't be reduced to how it is counted: there is always something in a person that fits into no box. In Theory of the Subject he lists anxiety and courage among the affects of the subject, and understands courage not as the absence of fear but as the capacity to hold your ground when you are afraid. You don't have to wait for the fear to disappear; you can take a very small step together with it.
social_anxiety.practice: Choose one tiny action for today — saying hello, asking a question — and do it, allowing yourself to feel nervous. Courage, for Badiou, is not the absence of fear.

uncertainty.text: Pascal proposed a wager — and Badiou takes up the thought: everything new begins with a bet made without guarantees. You want to know how things will end, and it's impossible to know — that is hard. Badiou argues that this is exactly how everything genuinely new works. An event, in his view, is "undecidable": at the moment it happens, it can't be proven that it matters or where it will lead. Uncertainty doesn't mean you prepared badly or are living wrongly. It is the common condition of any beginning: in love, in work, in changing your life. Badiou calls the work that follows an event "fidelity", and this fidelity doesn't require knowing the outcome in advance. It requires only the next step.
uncertainty.practice: Imagine three outcomes — a good one, a bad one and one in between — and find one small step that makes sense in all of them. Take it today.

waiting.text: Badiou loved Beckett for characters who keep walking and talking no matter what: he saw in them not despair but the stubborn strength of desire. Waiting — for results, an answer, news — stretches time, and focusing is hard. Badiou distinguishes what doesn't depend on us from what we do in response. A committee's decision, a phone call, a diagnosis — all of this comes from outside, and you can't influence it. But the life of a subject, for Badiou, is built not out of waiting for a verdict but out of fidelity to what is dear to you: people, a cause, a thought. While the answer hasn't come, there is something that goes on regardless of it. Waiting does not cancel your life.
waiting.practice: Say slowly the ending of Beckett's The Unnamable: "…you must go on, I can't go on, I'll go on." Then do one small thing that matters whatever the answer.

regret.text: "Reactivation" is one of Badiou's most hopeful concepts: a truth, once it has appeared, doesn't vanish without a trace. Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again, and it is a sign that something mattered to you. In Logics of Worlds, Badiou describes moments of choice as "points" where the world demands a simple "yes" or "no", and he admits that people sometimes back away. But a truth, for Badiou, can be returned to later, in other circumstances, in another form. A missed opportunity isn't closed forever: what was precious in it — courage, love, a cause — can come alive in your life in a different way. Regret then becomes not a verdict but a memory of what you still want to be faithful to.
regret.practice: Name in one word what was precious in what you missed: courage, closeness, a cause. Then imagine where that word could appear in your week, even in another form.

longing.text: Whoever has once looked at the world from the point of view of the Two, Badiou writes, no longer sees it as before. That is why it is precisely this person's voice, gaze and presence you miss so sharply. In In Praise of Love, Badiou describes love as a "scene of the Two": an experience in which the world is seen from two points of view at once. Longing is the scene of the Two continuing in absence: you still see the world through that person's eyes too, and so their absence is felt everywhere. It hurts, but it is also evidence that the encounter was real. Badiou says that a truth born in love doesn't vanish without a trace. Longing is one form of fidelity, and you don't have to hurry it.
longing.practice: Look at something the way this person would — the sky, the street, a bookshelf — and notice that you are seeing it through their eyes. This is the part of the "scene of the Two" that has stayed with you.

world_pain.text: Humanity, for Badiou, doesn't end at the borders of your own circle: truths are addressed to everyone. When hard news, war and injustice hurt you, it shows that you care about what happens to people you will never meet. It is a precious feeling, though hard to carry. But in Ethics he also warns about something else: when people turn into nothing but victims on a screen, and we into helpless spectators, compassion easily becomes passive and draining. Such pain is easier to carry if it is tied not only to the stream of images but also to something you can do in your own world — help, support, be there. Even a small action changes the position of the spectator.
world_pain.practice: Limit your time with the news today and do one concrete small act of care for someone near you. For Badiou, this is a way out of the spectator's position.

rejection.text: "Love without risk" is what dating services promised, and in In Praise of Love Badiou argues with that promise. Rejection wounds as if you had been refused not one thing but yourself as a whole. For him, meeting another person is always risky, and that is its value: love begins with a chance that can't be guaranteed. Rejection is the price of the risk you took by opening up to another person. It is not proof of your insignificance but a trace of your courage. The encounter didn't become a "scene of the Two", but your capacity for encounter hasn't gone anywhere. Rejection closes one door, but it doesn't make you someone incapable of loving and being loved.
rejection.practice: Place a palm on your chest and say to yourself under your breath: "I opened up — and that was brave." For Badiou, the capacity for encounter can't be taken away by a refusal.

abandonment.text: Love, Badiou admits, comes with no guarantees: it is neither a contract nor an insurance policy. That is why the fear of being abandoned can live in the body constantly, even when everything seems fine — behind it lies a deep need for a reliable bond. That is precisely why it requires fidelity — a daily carrying-on that no one can secure in advance. The fear of abandonment is the flip side of how much the lastingness of a bond means to you. But Badiou also offers another support: a subject is held up not only by someone holding on to them, but also by their own fidelity — to people, a cause, a thought. That fidelity belongs to you, and no one can take it from you.
abandonment.practice: Name aloud three things you are faithful to regardless of other people, folding a finger for each. This, for Badiou, is a support no one can take from you.

unrequited.text: "The scene of the Two" cannot be built alone — Badiou stresses this again and again. When you love without being loved back, the strength of the feeling joins its impossibility, and that is agonizing. For Badiou, love in the full sense is a "scene of the Two", a construction that two people create together. In unrequited love the encounter happened on one side only, and the Two did not come together. This is neither a mistake nor a fault: such a construction simply can't be built alone, however strongly you love. But what you have lived through is not empty. Badiou says that love is an experience of the world from the point of view of difference, and you have already learned how strongly you can be taken hold of by another person. That capacity remains yours, even if this person did not respond.
unrequited.practice: Sit quietly for a minute and let yourself feel how strongly you are capable of being taken hold of by another person — not for their sake, but for yours. That capacity, Badiou would say, remains yours.

humiliation.text: "The Immortal" is Badiou's name for what in a human being is greater than the circumstances they are put in. Someone tried to make you smaller than you are, and this pain is serious. In Ethics, Badiou objects to seeing a person only as a victim, a creature who can be humiliated and reduced to their vulnerability. Humiliation speaks about the situation and about those who humiliated you, but it passes no final verdict on you. It tries to put you in the box marked "nothing", but you don't fit in that box — no human being does. Your dignity is not cancelled by having been treated badly.
humiliation.practice: Stand up, square your shoulders and slowly lift your head, as if reclaiming your height. Name to yourself one thing you value in yourself that this event cannot cancel.

body_shame.text: A body, for Badiou, matters because it can carry a truth into the world: hug, work, create, be there for someone. If you dislike your body right now, it can easily colour a whole day, and there is nothing shameful in that. Badiou, following Lacan, criticizes the "service of goods" — a life in which everything, bodies included, is assessed like merchandise against a market standard. Dissatisfaction with the body is often born right there: in comparison with a model designed so that you won't match it. The value of the body lies not in meeting a standard but in the fact that through it you take part in life. This doesn't require you to love it straight away — only to see it from another side.
body_shame.practice: Make one movement your body enjoys — stretch, roll your shoulders, knead your palms — and silently thank it for one thing it helped you do today.

illness.text: Beckett, whom Badiou admired, wrote characters barely able to move — and yet they carry on: talking, desiring, searching. When your body lets you down, the world narrows and your strength drains — it is hard, and you have every right to be tired and upset. Badiou argued with philosophies that define a human being above all through vulnerability and mortality. He doesn't deny the fragility of the body, but says a person can't be reduced to it: there is in us a capacity to be faithful to love, to thought, to people — and that fidelity doesn't depend on how healthy the body is. Illness changes the forms of your life but doesn't cancel what is dear to you. Sometimes fidelity simply means carrying on as far as you can today.
illness.practice: Give one minute to one thing that remains dear to you — a photo, a loved one's voice on the phone, the view from the window — and simply be with it, asking nothing more of yourself.

quote.text: …you must go on, I can't go on, I'll go on.
quote.author: Samuel Beckett

pride.text: Badiou valued not so much the flash of inspiration as the work that comes after it. Pride in what you have done is a good, well-earned feeling, and there's no need to be embarrassed by it. In Theory of the Subject, Badiou names courage and justice among the affects of the subject: they are what a person experiences when holding fast in fidelity to their cause. And in later texts he speaks of "real happiness" — the joy that comes from taking part in something greater than survival. Healthy pride is a sign that for a while you were a subject, not just someone who completed a task: you showed persistence, saw it through, stayed faithful to what you set out to do. Let yourself enjoy the pride — it confirms that such fidelity is within your reach.
pride.practice: Tell someone what you had to overcome to do this — not the result, but the path. Badiou would say you are telling the story of your fidelity.

melancholy.text: Badiou calls to action rather than contemplation, and he didn't write about melancholy specifically. But a quiet sadness mixed with tenderness doesn't need fixing — and there is room for it in his thought. If we continue his thought, melancholy is a sensitivity to what has no place in the habitual order of things. Badiou calls this order the "state of the situation": everything in it is counted, but not everything fits in it. Gentle sadness seems to remember that life is larger than what has been counted — past encounters, possibilities never realized. And his idea of "reactivation" says that a past in which there was something genuine can come alive again. Melancholy, then, is not a dead end but a careful keeping of what may yet return.
melancholy.practice: Spend a couple of minutes by a window or with quiet music and ask yourself: which unrealized possibility is this tender sadness about?
